analysis.one_liner: Sets federal privacy rules requiring companies to secure personal data, get consent before sharing it, and notify people of breaches.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House subcommittee until the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created the first broad federal privacy law for commercial data. Companies holding data on more than 5,000 people would have had to keep that data secure, tell people what they collect and how they use it, get permission before sharing it for advertising, let people see and correct their records, and notify anyone whose data was exposed in a breach. A second part would have updated the children's online privacy law for the smartphone era, covering mobile apps, restricting targeted ads to kids and teens, and limiting collection of children's location data. It was introduced in May 2014, sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the two-year congressional term ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who use websites, apps, and online services. The bill would have given everyone clearer notice of what companies collect about them, a say before their data is used for targeted advertising or sold to third parties, security obligations on the companies holding their data, prompt notice and free credit reports after a breach, and stronger protections for children's and teens' data — including restrictions on location tracking and targeted marketing to minors under 16, and a way to erase personal content kids have posted. People harmed by identity theft and data breaches stood to gain the most, since breaches were common and notification rules were a patchwork of state laws.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Internet users and families with kids

how_it_helps.text: It would have required the FTC to write rules forcing companies that hold data on more than 5,000 people to secure that information, and to notify people when their personal data is exposed in a breach.

Companies would have to tell people what they collect and why, get opt-in consent before using data for behavioral advertising or handing it to third parties, and let people see and correct what is stored about them.
It would have limited collection to what is reasonably necessary, restricted how long data is kept, and barred third parties from re-identifying supposedly anonymous data without consent.

For children and teens, it would have extended the children's privacy law to mobile apps, banned targeted marketing to kids without parental or teen consent, restricted collection of children's location data, and required an 'erase' button for content kids post publicly.

Breach victims would have been entitled to free credit reports, and breaches involving more than 10,000 people would have to be reported to a federal entity that shares them with the FBI, Secret Service, FTC, and state attorneys general.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that collect, trade, and monetize personal data — online advertisers, data brokers, app makers, and any business handling data on more than 5,000 people. They would have faced compliance costs for security, notice, consent, and record-keeping, plus FTC penalties up to $6 million for reckless or repeated violations, and would have lost the freely available behavioral-advertising data that funds much of the free internet. Some of those costs would likely have been passed to consumers, and small businesses would have gotten waivers where compliance costs were excessive.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers, advertisers, and app makers

drawbacks.text: The bill would have supersede state privacy laws covering the collection, use, and disclosure of covered information, wiping out stronger protections in states like California in favor of a single federal standard.

It explicitly provided no private right of action, so individuals could not sue companies that misused their data; only the FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general could enforce the rules.

It created 'safe harbor' programs run by nongovernmental organizations in which participating companies would be exempt from core notice and consent requirements, a form of industry self-regulation the bill's own findings criticized.

Companies could exempt themselves from breach notification if they concluded there was no reasonable risk of identity theft or fraud, and the bill put pre-notification constraints on credit-card-only breaches, weakening the notice consumers would receive.
Civil penalties were capped at $6 million per related series of violations, a sum that is small for the largest data companies, and enforcement required showing reckless or repeated violations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits were substantial and concrete: a national floor for data security, honest notice about what is done with personal information, opt-in consent before third-party tracking, a right to see and correct stored data, reliable breach notification with free credit reports, and a real update to children's privacy for the smartphone era. The costs are real but manageable: compliance expenses for businesses, passed through to consumers only marginally, and some rules might have been written clumsily by a first-generation FTC rulemaking. The genuine design flaws are that the bill preempted state privacy laws, relied on industry-run safe harbor programs that could water down enforcement, allowed companies themselves to declare breaches harmless, capped penalties, and gave individuals no right to sue on their own. On balance, the protections for people outweighed those flaws, but the flaws are exactly what a fair observer would have wanted fixed before passage.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, passed down to a subcommittee, and never heard from again before the term expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Albio Sires introduced H.R. 4711 on May 21, 2014, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On May 23, 2014, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade, where no further action was taken.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred; the bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
The bill attracted only two cosponsors, both Democrats, and never developed the bipartisan backing that privacy legislation typically needs to reach the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that profit from collecting, trading, and targeting advertising with personal data were better off, since no federal privacy or breach-notification rules were imposed on them. Americans' data stayed governed by a patchwork of state laws and voluntary industry practices.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without any hearing, markup, or vote from referral in May 2014 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade
against.what_they_did: Received the bill two days after introduction and took no action on it.

against.name: Internet, advertising, and data-broker industries
against.role: Companies whose business depends on collecting and monetizing consumer data
against.what_they_did: The commercial data industry has consistently lobbied against comprehensive federal privacy legislation of this kind.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and two Democratic cosponsors, but no opposition was ever recorded because no hearing or vote ever took place.

industries.industry: Data brokers and behavioral advertising companies
industries.note: These firms' business is compiling and selling detailed profiles of individuals. The bill would have required opt-in consent before data was used for behavioral advertising or transferred to third parties and restricted re-identification of 'anonymous' data, cutting into core revenue.

industries.industry: Internet platforms, websites, and mobile app makers
industries.note: The bill imposed security duties, transparent notice, data minimization, and retention limits on any entity holding data on more than 5,000 people, and extended children's privacy rules to mobile apps, including a ban on targeting kids with ads without consent. Compliance would cost money and restrict common data practices.

The bill required companies to notify major credit bureaus of large breaches and to arrange free consumer credit reports for breach victims, giving the bureaus a notification role and a service obligation rather than a new revenue stream.

The bill directed the FTC to set up 'safe harbor' programs administered by nongovernmental organizations, under which participating companies would be exempt from key requirements — creating a new industry-funded self-regulation role.
